Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
try hard not think about the trauma
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: John is a 36-year-old European male who works at a local retail store. He has been married for ten years and lives in a suburban area with his wife and two young children. John experienced a traumatic event-a man-made disaster at his workplace-over three months ago, which profoundly impacted him. The day of the disaster was a typical workday until it wasn't. A fire broke out suddenly, engulfing the store and forcing employees to flee for their lives. The panic and chaos were overwhelming, and John found himself in close proximity to individuals who were behaving erratically, screaming and pushing others as they tried to escape. In the midst of this chaos, he felt a distinct texture on his skin that he now associates with danger-a rough, scratchy sensation that reminded him of the burning debris around him. Since then, any physical closeness or tactile sensations reminiscent of that day trigger intense reactions in John. When his coworkers come too close or when he feels a specific texture, like the rough fabric of certain clothing items, it immediately brings back vivid memories of the fire and the panic. These triggers are so potent because they transport him right back to the moment of the disaster. To cope with these intrusive thoughts and feelings, John has developed several maladaptive strategies. He often tells himself that the event did not really happen or was not as bad as he remembers it, trying to diminish its impact on his psyche. When this doesn't work, he tries to suppress the memories entirely, pushing them away from his conscious mind. However, when these thoughts do surface, they feel more real and vivid than any other memory he has, which only intensifies his shame. The memory of the event is so visceral that John recalls it as a series of snapshots-discrete moments frozen in time that replay themselves in his mind with alarming clarity. Each snapshot feels like a snapshot from a movie reel, with specific details etched into his brain: the sound of shattering glass, the smell of smoke, and the faces of panicked individuals. These snapshots are so vivid that they often lead him to engage in self-harm as a way to distract himself from the overwhelming emotions. John's shame intensifies when he remembers these moments, making it difficult for him to leave his house or interact with others without feeling intense anxiety. The memories have become intertwined with the triggers he experiences, creating a cycle where one feeds into the other. For instance, if he touches something that feels rough, like the texture of the debris during the fire, he immediately recalls those snapshots and feels compelled to hurt himself physically as a way to escape. This cycle has taken a toll on his work life. He has become increasingly avoidant at his job, often finding excuses to stay away from areas where he might feel physically close to others or come into contact with similar textures. His colleagues have noticed his withdrawal and growing irritability, leading to strained relationships at work. What finally brought John to seek help was a particularly intense episode that occurred when he was shopping for groceries. He felt the rough texture of the shopping cart handle and was immediately transported back to the disaster. Overwhelmed by shame and anxiety, he became unable to function and realized he needed professional intervention to break this cycle. Despite his fears, John is hoping that therapy can help him reclaim control over his life and stop reliving those terrifying moments. John's journey has been marked by a relentless battle against these intrusive memories and the overwhelming triggers they bring. His maladaptive strategies have only served to exacerbate the problem, creating a self-reinforcing loop where his memories feel more real than anything else in his life. He is now at a critical point, hoping that with professional guidance, he can find a way to move past this trauma and regain some sense of normalcy.
